exercises.prompt: In which division do you declare a data item such as `01 total PIC 9(5)V99.`?

options.label: The identification division
options.feedback: Not yet. The identification division names the program (`PROGRAM-ID`) and little else.

options.label: The environment division
options.feedback: Not yet. The environment division connects the program to files, devices and local conventions such as `DECIMAL-POINT IS COMMA`.

options.label: The data division
options.feedback: Yes. Every data item is declared in the data division, here in its `WORKING-STORAGE SECTION`, before the procedure division may use it.

options.label: The procedure division, just before the first use
options.feedback: Not yet. COBOL never declares data among the statements; the procedure division only works on items laid out in advance.

hints: COBOL separates describing data from using it.
exercises.solution: The **data division**. A program lays out every item it uses, with its size and format, in the data division (working storage, file records, linkage items). The procedure division may then refer to those items but never declares new ones.

exercises.prompt: Name the four divisions a COBOL program can have, one word each (for example `identification`).
hints: One names the program, one connects it to the outside world, one describes its data, one does the work.
exercises.solution: **Identification, environment, data, procedure**, always in that order. Only the identification division is strictly required, but every useful program also has a procedure division.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about COBOL's origins is accurate?

options.label: Grace Hopper wrote COBOL alone at IBM in 1957.
options.feedback: Not yet. Hopper worked at Remington Rand, not IBM, and COBOL was designed by a committee; she advised it and her FLOW-MATIC was its main model.

options.label: A committee of manufacturers, users and government agencies (CODASYL) designed it in 1959, drawing above all on Hopper's FLOW-MATIC.
options.feedback: Yes. The May 1959 meeting at the Department of Defense launched the effort, and the COBOL-60 specification followed in 1960.

options.label: It was designed by mathematicians as a successor to FORTRAN for scientific computing.
options.feedback: Not yet. COBOL was designed for business data processing: records, files and decimal money. FORTRAN served scientific computing.

options.label: It was created during the year-2000 crisis to fix date bugs.
options.feedback: Not yet. COBOL was forty years old by then; the year-2000 work fixed date logic *in* existing COBOL programs.

hints: The C in CODASYL stands for Conference.
exercises.solution: COBOL was specified by a **CODASYL committee** formed after a meeting at the US Department of Defense in May 1959. Its most direct ancestor was **FLOW-MATIC**, the English-like UNIVAC language developed by Grace Hopper's team; IBM's COMTRAN also contributed. The first specification, COBOL-60, appeared in 1960.

exercises.prompt:
What is the **last** line this program prints?

```cobol
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. nines.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 n        PIC 99  VALUE 9.
01 i        PIC 99.
01 product  PIC 999.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM VARYING i FROM 2 BY 2 UNTIL i > 6
        MULTIPLY n BY i GIVING product
        DISPLAY n " x " i " = " product
    END-PERFORM
    STOP RUN.
```

feedback.message: Not yet: `DISPLAY` shows every digit of a `PIC 99` or `PIC 999` item, including leading zeros.
Not yet: the test `i > 6` is made before each pass, so the loop stops when `i` becomes 8.

hints: `i` takes the values 2, 4, 6, then 8, and the condition is tested before each pass.
`n` is `PIC 99`, `i` is `PIC 99` and `product` is `PIC 999`: how many digits does each show?
exercises.solution: The loop runs for `i` = 2, 4 and 6 and stops when `i` = 8 makes `i > 6` true. The last pass computes 9 × 6 = 54. `DISPLAY` shows numeric items with all their digits, so the line is **`09 x 06 = 054`**.

exercises.prompt:
How many lines does this program print?

```cobol
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. q.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "Kia ora" " " "COBOL"
    DISPLAY "Line two"
    STOP RUN.
    DISPLAY "Line three".
```

feedback.message: Not yet: what does `STOP RUN` do to the statements after it?
Not yet: one `DISPLAY` with several operands prints them all on one line.

hints: A `DISPLAY` with three operands prints one line.
exercises.solution: **2.** The first `DISPLAY` joins its three operands into one line, `Kia ora COBOL`; the second prints `Line two`. `STOP RUN` then ends the run, so `Line three` is never displayed. The compiler accepts the unreachable statement without complaint.

exercises.prompt: In fixed-format COBOL, in which column do you put `*` to make a whole line a comment?

feedback.message: Not yet: columns 1 to 6 are the sequence area, kept for line numbers.
Not yet: column 8 is the start of Area A, where division and paragraph names begin.

hints: Six columns are reserved for card sequence numbers first.
exercises.solution: **Column 7**, the indicator area. Columns 1 to 6 hold sequence numbers, column 7 holds `*` (comment), `-` (continuation) or `D` (debugging line), Area A is columns 8 to 11, Area B is 12 to 72, and 73 to 80 are ignored.

exercises.prompt: `cobc` reports `syntax error, unexpected FULL` on a line that says `DISPLAY full`, although `01 full PIC 9 VALUE 3.` is declared. What is the best fix?

options.label: Rename the item to something like `ws-full` or `full-count`.
options.feedback: Yes. `FULL` is a reserved word in GnuCOBOL, so it cannot name data. A hyphenated or prefixed name can never collide with a keyword.

options.label: Write it in capitals, `FULL`, so the compiler recognises it.
options.feedback: Not yet. COBOL is case-insensitive; `FULL` and `full` are the same reserved word.

options.label: Add a full stop after `DISPLAY full`.
options.feedback: Not yet. The problem is the name, not the punctuation; the error would remain.

options.label: Compile without `-free`.
options.feedback: Not yet. Fixed format would bring new column errors and the reserved word would still be reserved.

exercises.solution: `FULL` is one of GnuCOBOL's more than a thousand reserved words. Rename the item (`ws-full`, `full-count`). Many shops prefix working-storage names with `ws-` partly for this reason.
